items.text: In Busan, South Korea, a 3.5-meter shark has been stuck in a narrow port canal for over two weeks after a second rescue attempt failed. Rescuers tried using a massive 50-meter net to gently herd the animal back out toward the open ocean; however, the operation had to be called off when the net kept snagging on underwater rocks. The shark, believed to be a bronze whaler, has turned into a major local celebrity, and it drew roughly 600,000 visitors to the canal area. Marine experts think noisy surroundings and city lights might be confusing the shark’s senses and make it hard for the animal to navigate out on its own. Rescuers have now positioned the net to keep the animal close to the sea. They hope changing tides will help it swim home. Meanwhile, researchers note that rising sea temperatures are driving significantly more large sharks toward South Korea’s coastlines. Difficult words: herd (to gather and guide animals or people to move together in a specific direction), snag (to catch or get caught on something sharp or rough). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

A large 3.5-meter shark got stuck in a canal in Busan, South Korea, more than two weeks ago. People gave the shark the nickname Bukangi, and around 600,000 visitors came to see it. Rescue teams tried to guide the shark back to the open ocean twice with the help of water jets and a large 50-meter net. The second rescue attempt failed on Friday because the net got caught on sharp rocks. Experts believe city noise and bright lights are confusing the shark, which finds it difficult to get into the sea. Rescue teams left a net barrier to stop it from swimming deeper into the city. They hope the ocean currents will help it swim out naturally. Scientists say warmer sea waters are bringing more large sharks near South Korea. Difficult words: water jet (a strong, fast stream of water pushed out with strong force), attempt (trying to do something difficult or achieve a goal), current (a movement of water flowing in a specific direction). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

A big shark is stuck in a canal in South Korea. The shark is over three meters long. It is in the canal for three weeks now. Local people call the shark Bukangi. Many people go to watch it swim. Rescuers try to help the shark go back to the sea. They use a big net, but the net hit rocks. Experts say that city lights and noise confuse the shark. It cannot find its way out. Rescuers now hope that the ocean water will help the shark swim home naturally . Scientists say warmer seawater brings more sharks near the country. Difficult words: stuck (when you cannot move or get out of), confuse (when someone cannot think clearly or understand a situation), naturally (when something happens without any help). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Swiss voters have clearly rejected a proposal that wanted to enforce super strict rules on the country’s traditional neutrality. Backed by a right-wing party, the plan tried to ban military cooperation with groups like NATO and stop Switzerland from placing sanctions on nations at war. However, over two-thirds of voters said no. They prefer to give the government room to maneuver . The result really shows people are happy with the status quo rather than looking for a big political shift. Voters basically support how the government reacted after Russia invaded Ukraine. Switzerland has kept close ties with European neighbors and backed sanctions against Russia. While this result doesn’t mean a total defeat for the right-wing party, it shows their momentum has stalled. Switzerland’s defense system works for now; however, an attack on a NATO country could still force everyone to rethink Swiss neutrality in the future. Difficult words: maneuver (to move or act skillfully to manage a tricky situation or get an advantage), status quo (the current state of things, without any changes), momentum (the force or speed that keeps a process or movement growing stronger over time). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

More than two-thirds of Swiss voters said no to a proposal for stricter rules on neutrality . A right-wing political party wanted to stop Switzerland from making agreements with NATO or using sanctions against countries at war. The Swiss government opposed the idea and said it would limit their choices during international conflicts. Swiss people prefer the current flexible situation, and they agree with how the government handled sanctions after Russia invaded Ukraine. They view neighboring European nations as natural allies . The vote shows that voters want the government to keep its current power to react to future global events. But if a war reaches a NATO country, Switzerland may need to change its rules again in the future. Difficult words: neutrality (the position of not taking any side in a conflict, war, or argument), oppose (to disagree with something or try to stop a plan or idea), flexible (able to change easily), ally (a person, group, or country that helps and supports another). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

People in Switzerland say no to new neutrality rules. Most people vote against an idea from a right-wing party. The new rules want to stop Switzerland from working with NATO or using economic sanctions during wars. The Swiss government wants to be free and decide how it needs to. People are happy with how things are now. Swiss people want to stay friends with other European countries and help Ukraine. Switzerland wants to keep its current system. But if a big war starts near Europe, Switzerland may have to think about its safety again. Difficult words: neutrality (when you do not take sides in a conflict or war), s anction (an official action against a country to stop its illegal actions), safety (when you are safe). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

As Brazil gets closer to its next election, the massive debt problem is getting way too big to ignore. Over 80% of households are deep in debt, mostly thanks to paying for everything in monthly installments , credit card rates shooting over 400%, and quick loans on banking apps. On top of that, a huge surge in online sports betting has made financial stress even worse for regular families. Small businesses and farmers are also drowning in unpaid bills. Meanwhile, the government itself is struggling under heavy debt, with interest payments consuming over 8% of the national budget alongside mandatory spending on pensions and social programs. President Lula wants to keep spending money to help poor families, while his main rival Flávio Bolsonaro is promising cuts without offering detailed plans. Analysts warn that if whoever wins doesn’t implement difficult financial reforms, the whole economy could easily end up in a real slowdown . Difficult words: installment (one of several regular payments made over time to pay for something), mandatory (required by law or a rule), slowdown (a period when economic activity or growth becomes slower than before). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Brazil is preparing for a big election, but the country is dealing with serious debt problems. More than 80% of families owe money because of credit cards with very high interest rates. New phone apps, instant payment systems, and online gambling make it easier for people to borrow money and get into financial trouble. Many small businesses and farmers are also unable to pay back their bank loans . At the same time, the Brazilian government has huge debts and spends a lot of money on pensions and social programs to help poor people. President Lula wants to keep spending money to support families, while his main rival Flávio Bolsonaro promises to cut government spending. Economists warn that these heavy debts could cause the country’s economy to slow down soon. Difficult words: debt (an amount of money that you borrow and must pay back), instant (happening immediately), loan (money that a bank or person lends you, which you must return later). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Brazil has big debt problems before its new election. Most families owe money. They use credit cards and loans with high costs. Many people also lose money because they use mobile phones for online sports games. Small businesses and farmers cannot pay their banks either. The government also has big debts. It spends money on social programs and older people. President Lula wants to help families without money. His political rival wants to cut government spending to save money. Experts say that high debt is very bad for the economy. The next president must make big changes to help the country grow. Difficult words: debt (money which you borrow and must pay back), owe (to have to pay money to someone because they lend it to you), loan (money that a bank or person lends you, which you must return later), rival (a person who competes with somebody to win). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Basmati rice is one of the world’s most valuable rice varieties, and sells for up to twice the price of standard white rice. Both India and Pakistan grow this crop in the historical region of Punjab, which is now divided by an international border. For years, both nations have been locked in a legal dispute over the exclusive right to the Basmati name in the EU. Receiving Protected Geographical Indication (PGI) status would grant a valuable market monopoly , but neither country has been able to submit a joint application due to a lack of political cooperation. Although similar disputes, such as Halloumi cheese in divided Cyprus, were resolved through joint EU frameworks, negotiations between India and Pakistan have completely stalled . Without an agreement or EU protection, approximately 90% of rice sold globally under the name Basmati comes from other regions. Experts warn that if the EU delays its decision further it may destroy its protection completely. Difficult words: exclusive right (the official permission given to only one person or group to do or sell something), monopoly (complete control of a market or product by one single company or country), stall (to stop moving forward or making progress, often unexpectedly). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Basmati is a very expensive type of rice from the Punjab region, but this region is divided between India and Pakistan. Both countries want to protect the name Basmati in the EU to earn more money. If a name gets protection , other countries cannot use it. India asked the EU for special protection in 2018, and Pakistan asked in 2023. But the two countries don’t talk to each other, so they can’t make a shared decision. Other places, like Cyprus with Halloumi cheese, worked together with the EU to protect their product. But because India and Pakistan are not talking, almost 90% of Basmati rice sold around the world is not real. If the EU doesn’t act soon, the name Basmati might lose its special value completely. Difficult words: protection (legal rules which stop other people from stealing, copying, or harming a product or brand), shared (something that is used, owned, or done by two or more people or countries together), value (how important something is or how much money it costs). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Basmati is a famous and expensive rice. It grows in a place between India and Pakistan. This place is called Punjab. Both countries want the name Basmati for themselves in the EU. A special name brings a lot of money and protection . India asks the EU for the name first, and Pakistan asks later. But the two countries do not talk to each other to solve the problem. Because there is no rule yet, many companies sell fake Basmati rice around the world. Almost 90% of Basmati rice in shops does not come from Punjab. If Europe does not decide soon, the special name Basmati may not be important anymore. Difficult words: expensive (when something costs a lot of money), protection (rules which stop someone from stealing or copying a product), rule (an official instruction which tells you what you can or cannot do). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul and Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov held a brief 20-minute meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York. This marked the first direct diplomatic encounter between top German and Russian officials since Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine more than four years ago. The meeting took place despite escalating tensions, following German accusations that Russia orchestrated a drone attack at Leipzig/Halle airport. During the talks, Wadephul urged Moscow to abandon its dangerous path of escalation toward Germany, Europe, and NATO. While Lavrov downplayed the event’s importance and claimed Germany made no position changes, diplomats noted the symbolic weight of reopening a direct channel. Both sides disputed who initiated the exchange. Despite Germany’s primary role as a strategic supporter of Ukraine rather than a mediator, the meeting reflects broader shifts in diplomatic discussions as international leaders search for ways toward future negotiations. Difficult words: sideline (a place or occasion outside the main event where unofficial talks happen), orchestrate (to plan and organize a complex event or secret action carefully), downplay (to make something seem less important, serious, or bad than it actually is). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

German Foreign Minister met Russian Foreign Minister at the UN in New York. This was their first meeting since Russia invaded Ukraine over four years ago. The talks lasted only 20 minutes and happened during a time of high tension between both countries. Germany recently accused Russia of planning a drone attack at a German airport. The German minister told Russia to stop its dangerous actions against Europe and NATO. Russia said the meeting changed nothing, and both countries disagreed on who asked for the talk. Germany still strongly supports Ukraine with weapons and help. But this short meeting shows that leaders are starting to talk directly again as world organizations try to find peaceful solutions to end the war. Difficult words: tension (a feeling of fear or anger between people or countries), accuse (to say that someone did something wrong, illegal, or bad), peaceful (quiet and calm). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Top leaders from Germany and Russia meet in New York. This is their first talk in over four years, since the start of the war in Ukraine. The meeting is only 20 minutes long. Relations are bad. Germany says that Russia tries a drone attack on a German airport. The German leader asks Russia to stop dangerous actions in Europe. Russia says that the meeting does not change anything. Germany still helps Ukraine, but both countries decided to talk face to face. World leaders hope that these small talks can slowly help bring peace in the future. Difficult words: relation (how people or countries feel and act toward each other), action (what you do to achieve something), decide (to choose what to do after some thinking). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Scotland faces a severe national crisis. It recorded over 11,000 drug-related deaths in the past decade, which made it the drug death capital of Europe. In 2025 alone, 1,133 people died, driven by an increasingly dangerous supply of synthetic opioids like nitazenes. The origins of this crisis trace back to 20th-century industrial decline, poverty, and intergenerational trauma . Additionally, political decisions worsened the situation, including controversial 2015 funding cuts to treatment services by the Scottish government, for which officials have since apologized. To combat the epidemic, Scotland is expanding its national drug testing facilities to identify rapid market changes and provide scientific evidence for public health policies. Police continue seizing tens of millions of kilograms worth of illicit substances, while politicians advocate for harm-reduction measures, including safer consumption rooms and expanded rehabilitation spaces. Some facilities offer critical recovery programs, which give long-term users a safe environment to overcome addiction and rebuild their lives. Difficult words: intergenerational trauma (psychological pain or emotional stress passed down from parents or grandparents to their children and future generations), seize (to officially take control of illegal items or property using legal authority), illicit (forbidden by law, rules, or custom). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Scotland has a very big drug problem, with more than 11,000 drug deaths in ten years. Last year, 1,133 people died because new, dangerous synthetic drugs entered the market. This crisis started years ago when factories closed, and many people lost work, hope, or support. Past government decisions to cut funding for help services also made the crisis worse. Now, Scotland is trying to fix this health emergency. Scientists are testing new drugs to help health workers respond quickly. Police are stopping drug sellers, and the government is funding overdose treatments, rehab centers, and safer places for users. Recovery centers are helping people leave drugs behind. People who suffered from addiction can finally find a safe place to heal and start a new life. Difficult words: synthetic (made in a lab), funding (money given by an organization or government), overdose (taking too much drug or medicine), addiction (when you need to use or do something even if it hurts you). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Scotland has a big crisis . Over 11,000 people die from drugs in ten years. Last year, 1,133 people die because strong new drugs come to the country. The problem starts long ago when many people lose their jobs. They have no money. Political cuts to help centers also make things worse. Today, scientists test new drugs in a lab to keep people safe. Police work hard to stop dangerous drug sellers. The government now gives more money for doctors, medicines, and help centers. These centers help people stop using drugs and start a happy, safe life again. Difficult words: crisis (a difficult or dangerous time), cut (to reduce the money you give to someone to help), help center (a place which helps and gives medicine to people who need help). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Pregnancy-related complications claim a woman’s life every two minutes, with most deaths occurring in sub-Saharan Africa, notably Kenya. Limited access to healthcare facilities, especially in remote rural areas where 70% of the population resides, exacerbates the issue. Challenges include inadequate healthcare workers and transportation barriers to reach hospitals. However, innovative solutions are emerging, such as mobile ultrasound technology pioneered by organizations like Jakaranda Health and Google. This portable system, coupled with artificial intelligence, enables non- sonographers to perform scans, potentially saving lives by detecting pregnancy complications early. While still in trial phases, this advancement offers hope for improved maternal healthcare in Kenya, where only 10% of rural mothers currently have access to ultrasound services. Difficult words: exacerbate (to make a problem or bad situation worse), pioneer (to develop or be the first to use or apply something new), sonographer (a healthcare professional trained to perform ultrasound). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Every two minutes, a pregnant woman dies due to complications , mostly in places like Kenya. Many people in sub-Saharan Africa live far from hospitals. They don’t get good care and it is difficult to get to hospitals. But new technology, like portable ultrasound devices, may help. Groups like Jakaranda Health and Google create devices which non-experts can use. The devices use AI to analyze scans and detect problems early, which can save lives. Experts are still testing these devices which could greatly improve maternal healthcare in Kenya, where only a few mothers currently have access to ultrasounds. Difficult words: complication (a problem), portable (a thing which you can carry or move around), maternal (related to mothers). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Many pregnant women die. Some have problems during pregnancy . Some die when they give birth. In Africa, a pregnant woman dies every two minutes. It happens mainly in places like Kenya. Many people there live far from hospitals. They cannot get the right help. But now, there is a new device . It shows pictures of babies inside their moms. It is easy to use it. Even people who are not experts can do it. It can find problems early and save lives. Experts are still testing the device. But many people believe that it can make a big difference for women in Kenya. Difficult words: pregnant (a woman who has a baby inside her belly), pregnancy (the time when a woman has a baby inside her belly), device (a small machine which people use for a specific activity or work). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Micro-apartments are places that are very small, have very few amenities , very little space, and not many of the home comforts that you’d associate with living in a bigger apartment and certainly in a house. However, they’re becoming increasingly popular in the Japanese capital, particularly among younger people who’re just starting in the workplace and can’t afford rents for ordinary places, or they may be moving into Tokyo from out of town and want a cheap place to stay. Each micro-apartment measures just nine square meters, which is under half the size of a typical studio apartment in Tokyo. The benefit’s that there’s zero deposit and no ‘key money’, a nonrefundable gift to the landlord. Monthly rents range from 380 to 610 dollars, depending on where in Tokyo you are. Difficult words: amenity (a desirable or useful feature or facility of a building or place), nonrefundable (money that you pay and can’t get back). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

In the Japanese capital Tokyo, the so-called micro-apartments are a popular place for young people to live. These apartments have just nine square meters and they are very simple. There are very few amenities and very little space to keep just everything you need. Monthly rent is 380 to 610 dollars, and it depends on where exactly in Tokyo the apartment is. Micro-apartments are so popular with young people because they don’t have enough money for a bigger apartment. Many people come to live in Tokyo from other towns and they need a cheap place to stay. One benefit is that landlords don’t usually ask for any deposit . Difficult words: amenity (a good or useful thing about a place), landlord (a person who rents a building or apartment), deposit (money which someone gives to someone else as security). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Tokyo is the capital of Japan. Life in Tokyo is not cheap. Young people do not have enough money. They have their first job. Sometimes they come from small towns. They cannot rent a big apartment. They live in so-called micro-apartments. A micro-apartment is a very small apartment. It has just nine square meters. It is very simple. There are not many things. The monthly rent is between 380 and 610 dollars. The rent depends on where in Tokyo the apartment is. Young people prefer micro-apartments because they do not need to pay any deposit to the landlord . Difficult words: rent (to pay someone for the use of something, usually a car or apartment), deposit (money which someone pays as security), landlord (a person who has a building or apartment and someone else pays him or her for using it). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

A viral post by a user who lost a 2,061-day Duolingo streak exposed a fundamental flaw in the language-learning platform: years of daily app use failed to deliver actual conversational fluency. Duolingo achieved massive financial success; it reached 1 billion dollars in revenue in 2025. How? By prioritizing gamification features like notifications, streak freezes, and leaderboards. However, the company faced severe backlash after firing contractors to replace language courses with lower-quality generative AI content. This hyper-focus on user engagement over educational value eventually triggered a massive market correction. Duolingo’s stock plummeted roughly 80 percent from its peak near 544 dollars down to around 101 dollars by spring 2026. Investors grew skeptical as daily active user growth slowed, and law firms opened securities fraud investigations regarding potentially misleading growth metrics . The dramatic financial collapse demonstrated that while Duolingo successfully optimized user habits, push notifications, and short-term corporate revenue, it failed to teach users how to speak new languages fluently. Difficult words: gamification (the practice of adding game-like features, such as points, levels, or badges, to non-game activities to make them more engaging), hyper-focus (an intense, complete concentration on one specific goal, task, or feature while ignoring everything else), securities fraud (the illegal practice of lying, hiding facts, or giving false information to investors about a company’s financial health), metrics (data points used to track, evaluate, and assess performance or growth). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

A Duolingo user lost a 2,061-day streak and realized she still couldn’t speak Spanish fluently. This showed a big problem with the popular language app. Duolingo became very rich by using games, daily streaks, and notifications to keep people using the app every day. The company also replaced many human workers with cheap AI to build its courses, which made the lessons worse. Even though the company earned a lot of money, investors started to worry that users were not actually learning anything. The company’s stock price dropped by 80 percent by early 2026. Lawyers also started investigating the company for confusing investors about user growth . In the end, Duolingo created a great game to keep people clicking, but it failed at its main job: teaching people how to talk to real speakers. Difficult words: streak (a continuous period or unbroken sequence of doing a specific activity every single day), earn (to get money for work), user growth (the total number of people who use a product or service). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

A woman uses Duolingo for 2,061 days. She loses her daily streak. She can see that she still can not speak Spanish. Duolingo uses games, points, and notifications to make people use the app every day. The company also fires real teachers and uses AI computers to make quick lessons. But the lesson quality is bad. In 2026, the company loses a lot of money. People see that the app is not teaching real language skills . Duolingo builds a game, but it does not help people speak to others. Difficult words: fire (to make someone end in their job), quality (how good something is), skill (how well you can do something). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Chinese President Xi Jinping has completed a high-profile state visit to Washington to meet with US President Donald Trump. Despite red carpets, lavish dinners, and warm words between the leaders, the summit brought little political success. The two countries agreed to a brief two-month extension of a trade truce with lower tariffs; however, disputes remain regarding AI governance, trade, and Taiwan. Beijing stated that US military aid to Taiwan is an absolute red line. The visit was also marked by controversies: major news networks were temporarily banned from live White House coverage, and an official photograph of the leaders appeared to be edited using AI. However, China offered a gesture of goodwill by gifting two giant pandas to an Atlanta zoo. Experts note that while the visit stabilized communications between the world’s two largest superpowers, the true test of the relationship will depend on whether key trade and security issues are successfully resolved early next year. Difficult words: lavish (impressive, very expensive, or given in large, generous amounts), truce (a temporary agreement to stop fighting or arguing), gesture of goodwill (an action done to show friendly intentions, kindness, or respect). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Chinese President Xi Jinping visited President Donald Trump in Washington. The two leaders had a big dinner and shared friendly words, but they didn’t solve their main problems. They only agreed to stop new trade tariffs for two months. China wants the US to stop selling weapons to Taiwan, while the US wants better rules on AI and trade. There were also news problems because some TV reporters were not allowed inside the White House. People also noticed that an official photo of the leaders was edited . The biggest positive moment was when China promised to send two new giant pandas to a zoo in Atlanta. Experts say that even though the visit was friendly, it is still not clear if the two powerful countries can fix their biggest differences in the future. Difficult words: tariff (a tax on goods imported from another country), edited (changed or corrected), powerful (when you have great authority or control). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

President Xi Jinping from China visits President Donald Trump in the US. They have a big meal together and say friendly words. But they do not solve many big problems. The presidents have different ideas about money, AI, or Taiwan. They only agree to help trade for two short months. Another problem is with journalists . Some news companies can not show video of the visit. One photo of the presidents is edited . AI changes it. The visit was good for talking, but the two big countries still have many problems to solve together. As a friendly gift, China will send two new giant pandas to a zoo in Atlanta. Difficult words: meal (food which you prepare for one single sitting like breakfast or dinner), journalist (a person who writes about news stories), edited (changed). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Former Yes musician Rick Wakeman performed a live piano concert for 150 rescued moon bears at the Animals Asia sanctuary in Vietnam’s Tam Dao National Park. Wakeman played gentle, melodic original compositions on a grand piano set up near the enclosure perimeter to bring attention to the plight of Asiatic black bears in East Asia. The performance sought to highlight the remaining 125 bears still trapped in small cages on illegal bear bile farms, where about four animals die each month. In these facilities, bile is painfully extracted from the animals’ gallbladders for traditional medicine. Wakeman, a long-time supporter of animal welfare who has sponsored rescue bears since 2016, expressed deep concern over the cruel conditions the animals endure. He urged the Vietnamese government to quickly release the remaining captive bears so they can experience open space and proper care at the sanctuary before it is too late. Difficult words: plight (a dangerous, difficult, or very sad situation), bile (a bitter fluid produced by the liver that helps digest food), captive (kept in a space you cannot leave, without freedom). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Musician Rick Wakeman played a piano concert for 150 rescued bears in Vietnam. The performance took place outside at a large animal sanctuary in Tam Dao National Park. Wakeman wrote special gentle music to make the bears feel happy and calm. He wanted to help 125 other bears that are still kept in small metal cages on bile farms. People on these farms keep bears in tiny spaces and take liquid from their gallbladders for traditional medicine. Wakeman started supporting the sanctuary in 2016 and even adopted a young bear. He hopes his music concert will help people understand the problem and convince the government to move the rest of the bears from the farms to the safe sanctuary soon, where they can run, play, and live on green grass. Difficult words: sanctuary (a safe place where animals are protected from harm), bile (a bitter fluid which helps process food in your body), gallbladder (a small organ in the body which holds and stores bile). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Rick Wakeman is a famous musician. He plays the piano for 150 bears at a big park in Vietnam. People save them from bad farms. On these farms, farmers keep bears in small cages . They use the bears for medicine. Wakeman plays soft music on a big piano to make the animals happy. He wants to help 125 more bears. These bears are still in small cages. Many of these sick bears die every month. Wakeman speaks to the government. He wants to save the animals fast so they can play on the green grass at the sanctuary . Difficult words: cage (a metal box in which people keep animals), sick (not well), sanctuary (a safe place where nothing bad can happen to you). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Malaysia’s Transport Minister Anthony Loke offered to resign from the cabinet in protest against a conditional royal pardon granted to jailed former Prime Minister Najib Razak. The pardon allows Najib to serve the remainder of his sentence under house arrest if he meets specific conditions, including paying a fine of approximately 12 million dollars. Loke, who serves as the Secretary-General of the Democratic Action Party (DAP), emphasized that keeping Najib behind bars is a firm boundary for the party due to its long-standing fight against corruption and commitment to justice. Despite Loke’s personal resignation offer, the DAP central executive committee decided that its four other ministers and seven deputy ministers will remain in government. DAP is the largest party in the ruling coalition. It holds 40 parliamentary seats and aims to protect political stability and prevent the collapse of the Prime Minister’s unity government. Loke assured the public that key national transport projects will continue without disruption. Difficult words: royal pardon (an official decision by a king or queen to forgive a person for a crime and reduce or cancel their punishment), commitment (a strong promise or firm decision to do something), executive committee (a small group of people who make important decisions for a larger organization or political party). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Malaysia’s Transport Minister offered to quit his government job. He is angry because the country’s king gave a special pardon to former Prime Minister Najib Razak. Under this new rule, Najib can leave prison and stay under house arrest if he pays a large fine. Loke said his party is strongly against corruption and believes that no one is above the law. But to keep the country’s government stable, only Anthony Loke offered to step down. Other ministers from his party will stay in their posts so the Prime Minister’s government doesn’t fall. Loke promised that big national transport projects will continue as planned without any problems. Difficult words: pardon (when a guilty person is officially freed), house arrest (when a person is forced to stay inside their own home instead of going to prison), corruption (when people in power do illegal things). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

An important politician in Malaysia, Anthony Loke, wants to quit his job as transport minister . He is unhappy because ex leader Najib Razak can leave prison to live at home under house arrest . Anthony Loke says that all people must follow the law. His political party is very big and strong. Other ministers in his party will stay in the government . They want to keep the country safe and stable so the government does not end. Loke says that public buses and train projects will keep working normally. Difficult words: transport minister (the top politician who cares about roads and public travel infrastructure), house arrest (when a person must stay at home instead of in prison), government (a group of people who run a country). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

London’s real estate market is facing a severe slump in flat sales, which is in sharp contrast with the high demand seen just a few years ago. Property data reveals a growing mismatch in the housing crisis: 88 percent of flats listed for sale in London last year failed to find a buyer within six months. High mortgage rates, rising service charges, and changing post-pandemic preferences for larger living spaces have combined to make flats far less attractive compared to houses. Complex leasehold structures, ongoing maintenance issues, and unresolved building defects further paralyze the market. Residents in Croydon are left without hot water or heating due to gas leaks, yet they cannot sell their properties because management companies clash over repair bills. Meanwhile, unresolved fire safety regulations following the Grenfell tragedy leave thousands of buildings with unsafe cladding , which prevents owners from selling. The UK government is introducing measures to cap ground rents and speed up cladding removal to help restore stability. Difficult words: slump (a sudden and severe drop or decline in price, value, sales, or economic activity), mismatch (a failure to correspond or fit together well), paralyze (to cause something to stop functioning, moving, or operating normally), cladding (a covering or outer layer of material added to the outside walls of a building). The doorway effect , also known as the location updating effect, is a common memory lapse that occurs when walking into a new room makes you forget your original intention. Psychologists explain that our brains break continuous time into separate events. When moving through a doorway or entering a new space, the brain identifies an event boundary . It saves the previous event model into long-term memory and clears short-term memory to prepare for incoming information, and sometimes accidentally erases thoughts you still need. Scientific experiments using physical and virtual environments show that passing through doorways slows response times and increases forgetting, especially when people are multitasking. Similar memory lapses can be triggered by changing computer tabs, time jumps in stories, or sudden distractions. However, event boundaries can also help organize information by preventing interference between tasks. To recover lost thoughts, scientists suggest retracing your physical steps or consciously repeating your goal as you move between spaces. Difficult words: lapse (a temporary failure or brief drop in concentration, memory, or judgment), boundary (a line, point, or limit that marks where one thing ends and another begins), interference (a situation where new or different information blocks or disrupts your ability to remember something clearly). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

The doorway effect happens when you walk into a new room and suddenly forget what you were going to do. Scientists explain that our brains divide our daily life into different events. When you go through a door, your brain thinks a new event is starting. It clears your short-term memory to make space for new information, which can make you forget your previous thought. Studies show that passing through doorways makes people forget things more easily, especially when they are multitasking or moving through many rooms. Similar things happen when you change tabs on a computer or get distracted. To remember what you forgot, you can walk back to the previous room or repeat your goal out loud while moving. Difficult words: divide (to separate something into smaller parts), short-term memory (the part of your brain which holds a small amount of information for a few minutes), multitask (to do or try to manage more than one activity at the same time). A major scientific study reveals that Greenland and Antarctica have lost 12.5 trillion tonnes of ice since 1979. This massive loss has raised global sea levels by approximately 3.2 centimetres. Based on more than four decades of satellite observations, researchers found that while the ice sheets remained relatively stable through the 1970s and 1980s, melting accelerated significantly in the 1990s and reached its fastest rate during the 2010s. Rising air and ocean temperatures drive this destruction, with warmer seawater responsible for about 84 percent of the ice loss by melting glaciers from below. In Greenland, the Jakobshavn glacier is now retreating by up to 50 metres per day. Experts warn that for every centimetre of sea level rise, two to three million additional people face annual coastal flooding. Although ice loss temporarily slowed between 2020 and 2023 due to short-term weather patterns, scientists emphasize that the long-term melting trend continues. Difficult words: ice sheet (a massive layer of ice that covers a huge area of land), relatively (in comparison to something else), retreat (to move back or become smaller). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Difficult words: melting (when ice turns into liquid), ice sheet (a very big piece of ice which covers a large area), glacier (a large river of ice). Liberland is a self-proclaimed libertarian micro-state located on a small piece of land along the Danube between Croatia and Serbia. Founded in 2015 by Czech politician Vít Jedlička, the project takes advantage of an unresolved border dispute following the breakup of Yugoslavia. Jedlička aims to create a tax-free, digital state based on meritocracy , where financial contributions grant citizens greater political power than traditional democracy allows. This idea attracts global supporters who feel restricted by taxes and government control; however, Liberland faces severe practical and legal obstacles. Croatian authorities strictly guard the area, prohibit permanent settlement, and destroy unauthorized infrastructure. Furthermore, no sovereign country recognizes Liberland as an independent state. Visitors and prospective citizens, such as Italian project manager Antonella, view the project as an inspiring alternative to modern governments. However, critics describe it as a utopian experiment that exists as little more than a makeshift campsite on the riverbank. Difficult words: self-proclaimed (claimed or announced by oneself, without official confirmation, approval, or validation from others), meritocracy (a system or society where people gain power or influence based on their abilities and contributions rather than wealth or social background), sovereign (having full power and independent authority to govern itself without control from outside governments), utopian (aiming for an ideal, perfect society that is usually impossible to achieve in reality). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

In China, millions of people now pay for an app that asks them one simple question each day: “Are you dead?” The app targets people who live alone and worry that no one will notice if something bad happens to them. Users tap once a day to show they are safe. If they don’t respond for two days, the app sends a message to chosen contacts. Since it started last year, the app has become one of the most popular paid apps in the country. The app shows a big social change. More people in China live alone because fewer people marry, and many older adults live without family. Often, work contacts notice problems sooner than relatives . Experts say people feel more alone today, even though digital communication is everywhere. Studies show loneliness affects people of all ages. Online contact cannot fully replace a real human connection. Time with other people in real life still matters most for feeling connected and well. Difficult words: target (a person or group something is made for), relative (a family member), loneliness (feeling alone and disconnected). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Difficult words: notice (to see or realize something), social (about people and how they live together), loneliness (feeling alone and cut off). Snowflakes, with their intricate and captivating beauty, can be explained by the universal laws of nature. A snowflake, technically called a snow crystal, forms when water vapor meets tiny specks of dust or pollen in the clouds. This interaction creates a hexagonal structure with branching tips that attract more water molecules, resulting in the unique shape of each snowflake. Temperature and humidity determine the size and shape of these branches as the snowflake falls through the clouds due to gravity. No two snowflakes are alike due to their individual journeys. In 1611, Johannes Kepler theorized about the hexagonal pattern of snowflakes, which was later proven as an efficient use of space. Despite their white appearance, snowflakes are actually clear, with light scattering from their edges. Snowflakes, like celestial bodies, demonstrate the laws of physics and carry their unique history, much like humans. Difficult words: intricate (complex and detailed), captivating (capable of attracting and holding interest, charming), celestial (relating to the sky or universe). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Although snowflakes appear white, they are clear. Their symmetry is pleasing to the human brain, much like other symmetrical objects in nature. Snowflakes fall thanks to gravity and they follow universal laws of physics, just like objects in space. Photographing snowflakes requires perfect conditions and a lot of patience. Difficult words: vapor (mist or steam), humidity (how much water there is in the air), efficient (when something works perfectly without any waste), symmetry (when something is regular and its parts are in balance).
